chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a female slave whom the son of her master sold while his father was absent. The buyer had her bear a child (mawaliha), and she gave birth to a boy from him. Then the first master came and disputed with the second master, saying: 'My slave girl was sold by my son without my permission.' He said: 'The ruling is that he takes his slave girl and her son.' The one who bought her pleaded with him, saying: 'Take the son whom he sold you with the slave girl, until he completes the sale for you.' When he took him, the father of the boy said to him: 'Send my son.' He said: 'By Allah, I will not send you my son until you send my son.' When the master of the slave girl saw this, he ratified the sale of his son.

key_terms.اِسْتَوْلَدَهَا: To have her bear a child (mawaliha)
key_terms.خَاصَمَ: To dispute/argue in a legal context

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on a son selling his mother without the father's consent?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the principle of *al-khiyarat* (options) in Shia jurisprudence, specifically the father's right to ratify or reject his minor son's sale of a slave. Imam Ali’s ruling demonstrates a pragmatic legal mechanism where the buyer retains the purchased child as collateral (*habs*) to compel the father’s consent, thereby validating the transaction and clarifying the lineage and ownership status of the offspring.
